# Bayes factors versus ONS projection assumptions ::: {.cell} ::: This chapter compares the improvement rate that maximises the Bayes factor schedule for the **pre-pandemic headline window** (2011–2019, from the previous chapter) against the average annual improvement rate for $e_0$ implied by each ONS projection round (2012, 2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024) [@ons_expectation_of_life], to quantify how optimistic or pessimistic each projection has been relative to what the pre-2020 data alone implied. The Bayes-factor benchmark is a single value per population and sex: the mean annual $e_0$ gain at the pre-pandemic BF-maximising slowdown scenario. Anchoring on the pre-pandemic window (rather than a series that includes the COVID shock) keeps the comparison against ONS assumptions clean — the ONS rounds themselves are, likewise, projections of a smoothly improving process. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ch_e0_dta <- dta_e0 %>% group_by(population, sex) %>% arrange(year) %>% mutate(ch_e0 = e0 - lag(e0)) %>% ungroup() %>% filter(!is.na(ch_e0)) %>% select(-e0, -source) # Pre-pandemic (2011-2019) BF-maximising mean annual gain per population / sex. bf_benchmark <- ch_e0_dta %>% group_by(population, sex) %>% nest() %>% mutate(bf = map(data, ~calc_bayes_factors( .x, before_period = c(1991, 2010), after_period = c(2011, 2019), outcome_var = ch_e0))) %>% select(population, sex, bf) %>% unnest(bf) %>% group_by(population, sex) %>% slice_max(log_bf, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% ungroup() %>% transmute(population, sex, bf_mu = mu) bf_benchmark ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 10 × 3 population sex bf_mu 1 England female 0.103 2 England male 0.123 3 Northern Ireland female 0.119 4 Northern Ireland male 0.211 5 Scotland female 0.0683 6 Scotland male 0.112 7 United Kingdom female 0.0977 8 United Kingdom male 0.121 9 Wales female 0.0461 10 Wales male 0.0845 ``` ::: ::: For each ONS projection round we compute the mean annual improvement in period life expectancy at birth implied by that round (from the projection's period $e_0$ series in the projection year onwards), and set it alongside the pre-pandemic Bayes-factor benchmark. ::: {#tbl-bf-vs-ons .cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ons_implied <- ons_projections_tidied %>% mutate(sex = case_when( sex == "f" ~ "female", sex == "m" ~ "male", TRUE ~ NA_character_ )) %>% filter(age == 0) %>% filter(year >= proj_year) %>% group_by(country, sex, proj_year) %>% arrange(year) %>% mutate(ch_e0 = ex - lag(ex)) %>% summarise(ons_mu = mean(ch_e0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(country = ifelse(country == "UK", "United Kingdom", country)) %>% rename(population = country, round = proj_year) # Modern dplyr will not join a plain factor to an ordered factor, and mixing # population key types silently drops rows: coerce both sides to character # before the join (behaviour-preserving). combined_long <- ons_implied %>% mutate(population = as.character(population)) %>% left_join(bf_benchmark %>% mutate(population = as.character(population)), by = c("population", "sex")) %>% mutate(population = factor(population, levels = populations)) %>% arrange(population, sex, round) combined_wide <- combined_long %>% pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = c(ons_mu, bf_mu)) %>% select(population, round, ons_mu_female, bf_mu_female, ons_mu_male, bf_mu_male) %>% arrange(population, round) combined_wide %>% kable( digits = 3, col.names = c("Population", "Round", "ONS", "BF (pre-2020)", "ONS", "BF (pre-2020)") ) %>% add_header_above(c(" " = 2, "Female" = 2, "Male" = 2)) %>% kable_styling() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: The Bayes-factor benchmark (`BF (pre-2020)`) is constant down each population block, because it is the single pre-pandemic best estimate; the ONS column changes with each round. A round whose implied gain lies below the benchmark was projecting slower improvement than the pre-2020 data alone implied (relatively pessimistic); above it, relatively optimistic. Now a figure for the UK as a whole, showing every ONS round against the fixed pre-pandemic Bayes-factor benchmark. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} uk_long <- combined_long %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom") %>% select(round, sex, `ONS projection` = ons_mu, `Bayes Factor (pre-2020)` = bf_mu) %>% pivot_longer(c(`ONS projection`, `Bayes Factor (pre-2020)`), names_to = "method", values_to = "gain") %>% mutate(gain = 52.18 * gain) uk_long %>% ggplot(aes(x = round, y = gain, colour = method, shape = method, linetype = method)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~sex) + expand_limits(y = 0) + labs( x = "ONS projection round", y = "Implied gain (weeks/year)", title = "ONS-implied vs pre-pandemic Bayes-factor annual e0 gain", subtitle = "UK as a whole; Bayes-factor benchmark is fixed (pre-pandemic 2011-2019)" ) ggsave(here("bayes_paper", "figures", "M03_ons_cf_bayes_2024.png"), height = 12, width = 24, units = "cm", dpi = 300) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05_bf_vs_ons_files/figure-html/fig-ons-cf-bayes-1.png){#fig-ons-cf-bayes width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Reading down the UK block, the ONS rounds tracked steadily downwards from the 2012 round, reflecting the accumulating evidence of stalling: for UK females the implied gain fell from 0.152 years/year (2012 round) toward the pre-pandemic Bayes-factor benchmark of 0.098, and for males from 0.166 toward 0.121. The newer, post-drafting rounds (2020-based interim, 2022-based and 2024-based) sit close to the pre-2020 benchmark rather than far below it. For UK females the 2020, 2022 and 2024 rounds imply 0.110, 0.102 and 0.100 years/year respectively — all at or slightly **above** the pre-2020 benchmark of 0.098, i.e. marginally more optimistic than the pre-2020 data alone implied. For UK males the same rounds imply 0.132, 0.114 and 0.113, straddling the benchmark of 0.121 (the 2020 round slightly above, the 2022 and 2024 rounds slightly below). In short, the newest ONS rounds are broadly in line with — not markedly more pessimistic than — the pre-pandemic Bayes-factor estimate; the sharp downward revision happened over the 2012–2018 rounds, and has since levelled off. The remaining analysis expresses each ONS round and the pre-pandemic Bayes-factor benchmark as a proportion of the mean UK improvement from 1980 to 2010. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mean_lt_imp_uk <- dta_e0 %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom") %>% filter(between(year, 1980, 2011)) %>% group_by(sex) %>% arrange(year) %>% mutate(ch_e0 = e0 - lag(e0)) %>% summarise( mean_ch_e0 = mean(ch_e0, na.rm = TRUE), var_ch_e0 = var(ch_e0, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop" ) mean_lt_imp_uk ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 3 sex mean_ch_e0 var_ch_e0 1 female 0.197 0.0362 2 male 0.265 0.0237 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-est-as-pct-of-lt .cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lt_lookup <- mean_lt_imp_uk %>% select(sex, lt_ch_e0 = mean_ch_e0) est_as_pct_of_lt <- combined_long %>% filter(population == "United Kingdom") %>% select(round, sex, ONS = ons_mu, `BF (pre-2020)` = bf_mu) %>% pivot_longer(c(ONS, `BF (pre-2020)`), names_to = "method", values_to = "ch_e0") %>% left_join(lt_lookup, by = "sex") %>% mutate(new_as_pct = ch_e0 / lt_ch_e0) est_as_pct_of_lt %>% select(round, sex, method, new_as_pct) %>% unite(method, sex, col = "method_sex") %>% pivot_wider(names_from = method_sex, values_from = new_as_pct) %>% arrange(round) %>% kable(digits = 3) %>% kable_styling() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: And as a graph: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} est_as_pct_of_lt %>% ggplot(aes(x = round, y = new_as_pct, group = method, shape = method, colour = method)) + geom_point() + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~sex) + expand_limits(y = 0) + geom_hline(yintercept = 1) + labs(x = "ONS projection round", y = "Implied improvement as proportion of 1980-2010 UK trend") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](05_bf_vs_ons_files/figure-html/fig-est-as-pct-of-lt-1.png){#fig-est-as-pct-of-lt width=672} ::: ::: Two things stand out. First, from 2011 onwards both the ONS and the pre-pandemic Bayes-factor estimate sat well below the 1980–2010 long-run trend (the horizontal line at 1), confirming that the stalling was real and that the ONS, and the experts advising it, believed the long-run improvement rate was not sustainable. Second, whereas the original (2012–2018) analysis showed each biennial ONS round revising downwards and, for females, still potentially over-optimistic relative to the accumulating data, the extended series shows the ONS rounds levelling off close to the pre-pandemic Bayes-factor benchmark. With the corrected likelihood the evidence for a slowdown is in fact stronger for males than females (see the audit appendix), so the earlier suggestion that the ONS remained too optimistic *mainly* for females does not survive the update. An advantage of the Bayes-factor approach remains that it is trivial to re-run with each new annual data release, updating our beliefs about the underlying improvement rate within minutes of publication.
